I even have good reason to be content, because if he has not given me the perfection of being superior to error by the first means I noted above, which depends on clear and evident knowledge of everything I can deliberate about, he has at least left in my power the other means: to hold firmly to the resolution never to judge where the truth is not clearly known to me. For, although I am conscious of the weakness that I cannot keep my mind continually fixed on the same thought, I can nevertheless, by attentive and oft-repeated meditation, impress that resolution so strongly on my memory that I will never fail to recall it when I need it, and in this way I can acquire the habit of not erring.

7. It also strikes me that, to judge the perfection of the works of Deity, we should not look at one creature in isolation but at all his creatures together. For something that might perhaps, with some show of reason, seem highly imperfect if it were alone in the world may still be the most perfect possible when seen as a part of the whole universe. It was my purpose to doubt everything, and so far I know with certainty only my own existence and God's. Nevertheless, having noted the infinite power of Deity, I cannot deny that he may have produced many other objects, or at least that he is able to produce them, so that I may have a place as a part in relation to the great whole of his creatures.
